name: Gilgamesh: A New Rendering in English Verse
date: Farrar, Straus and Giroux hardcover, June 1992 (ISBN 9780374162276); FSG/Noonday paperback 1993 (ISBN 9780374523831), still in print. New York Times Notable Book; Ferry's first book after retiring from Wellesley.
creator: David Ferry (1924-2023), American poet and translator (later translator of Horace's Odes and Epistles, Virgil's Eclogues, Georgics and Aeneid), Sophie Chantal Hart Professor Emeritus of English at Wellesley College, National Book Award for Poetry 2012 for Bewilderment. Introduction by William L. Moran, Harvard Assyriologist.
form: Poet's verse rendering, not a line-by-line translation. Loose iambic pentameter laid out in unrhymed two-line stanzas (Ferry calls them 'iambic pentameter couplets'; the Ploughshares review calls them 'blank-verse couplets'), with occasional short lines set off at section openings (the poem begins with the single line 'The Story'). Organised by tablet, Tablets I to XII. Front matter: Moran's short introduction (about three pages per Danny Yee). Back matter: roughly seven pages of notes explaining Ferry's choices and liberties.
translator_access: Ferry did not read Akkadian or cuneiform. He worked from existing literal English translations, chiefly E. A. Speiser's version in Pritchard's Ancient Near Eastern Texts Relating to the Old Testament ('Speiser's translation, my main source'), plus word-for-word cribs supplied by his friend William L. Moran of Harvard for the opening passage and for Ishtar's proposal in Tablet VI. He argued the ignorance helped: 'I was working from scholarly word-for-word translations and these had the effect of being, in themselves, less nuanced and complex than I would have found the Babylonian, if I knew Babylonian' (interview with David Eckel, BU Core blog, 2010). He wrote it 'in a matter of months. Time of my life.'
scholarly_adviser: William L. Moran (1921-2000), Harvard Assyriologist and editor of the Amarna Letters, who supplied literal translations of key passages, encouraged the project and wrote the book's introduction.
versions_used: The Standard Babylonian (Nineveh) epic of eleven tablets plus the Akkadian Tablet XII, as mediated by Speiser's ANET translation (1950s) and Moran's cribs. Old Babylonian material comes in only where Speiser had already used it to fill the Standard Babylonian gaps (for example the Siduri speech on enjoying life, which survives only on the Old Babylonian Sippar/Meissner tablet). The Sumerian Gilgamesh poems are not used directly. Nothing post-1992 (no George 2003 edition, no Sulaymaniyah tablet). Ferry's name for the forest guardian is 'Huwawa', the older form, rather than Humbaba. [uncertain: exact list of secondary translations beyond Speiser and Moran not confirmed from the notes]
non_standard_material: Silent merge within the poem. No brackets, italics or typographic signals separate Standard Babylonian from Old Babylonian or from Ferry's own inventions; the reader has to turn to the endnotes to learn which passages are freely reworked, abridged or supplied. Ferry's notes acknowledge that the rendering takes many liberties with the surviving tablets and fragments. Tablet XII is kept as a separate, final tablet rather than woven into the narrative.
gap_policy: Bridged and smoothed. Ferry fills lacunae with plausible content of his own, or cuts across them, so the verse runs continuously. Danny Yee notes that when comparing a specific damaged passage across versions, 'in the Mason and Ferry versions these specific lines can't really be identified.' The endnotes, not the page, are where the gaps are admitted.
typography_of_absence: Essentially nothing. No square brackets, no editorial ellipses, no blank space for missing lines, and no line numbers. The page shows clean couplets with tablet headings; textual loss is invisible except through the notes. The odd bracket-free query in quotations circulating online (e.g. 'a meteorite(?)') appears to be inherited from Speiser-style wording rather than a systematic convention. [uncertain: not every page inspected]
tablet_xii: Included as the book's final tablet, after the return to Uruk in Tablet XI. Moran's introduction and Ferry's notes treat it as a separate, appended piece (an Akkadian rendering of part of the Sumerian 'Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Netherworld', in which Enkidu is alive again and descends to fetch the lost objects). The effect is that the book does not end on the walls of Uruk but on Enkidu's shade reporting the grim conditions of the dead, a darker, more elegiac close. [uncertain: exact framing of Tablet XII in Ferry's notes not verified verbatim]
turning_point: The death of Enkidu. Ferry named 'the heartbreaking death of Enkidu passage' as one of the parts that moved him most when he started, and the Tablet VIII lament, in which Gilgamesh mourns 'like a widow' over his friend, is one of the most concentrated stretches of the rendering. Everything after it becomes a flight from the knowledge of death. The poem's own opening already frames the story as a completed emotional arc rather than a tale of deeds: 'The Story / of him who knew the most of all men know; / who made the journey; heartbroken; reconciled;'. 'Heartbroken; reconciled' is Ferry's own compression of the Standard Babylonian prologue (which speaks of the king who saw everything, found out secrets and returned 'weary but at peace'), and it announces a hinge in grief and an ending in acceptance. The loss of the plant to the snake is a secondary hinge that finally forces the reconciliation.
arc_interpretation: Grief moving towards reconciliation, told with irony. Ferry's own summary of the hero lists the whole arc in one breath: 'such a wonderful terrifying, big-hearted, arrogant, scared, joyful, humiliated, sexy, desperate, grieving, self-deceiving, learning, heartbroken, reconciled character' (BU interview, 2010). The same pairing 'heartbroken; reconciled' sits in the poem's first lines, so the version reads as maturity reached through loss rather than as kingship or simple failure. Critics saw two registers. Joyce Peseroff (Ploughshares, Fall 1992) read Gilgamesh as both the first epic hero and the first anti-hero, whose 'Nietzschean' refusal of mortality ends with him returning home empty-handed, and stressed the poem's celebration of the city and of Enkidu's civilising. Tom Sleigh (New York Times Book Review) heard 'the hero's anguish' and 'the rage and despair of the untouchable'. Publisher copy says the pentameter captures the 'elegiac and ironic undertones' of a failed search for immortality. A lay reader (Jason McIntosh, Fogknife, 2017) even read it as black comedy about a vain demigod, which shows how much Ferry lets Gilgamesh's foolishness show. Because Tablet XII follows, the final note is less the consolation of the walls than a sober look at what death is like.
key_passages: Shamhat and Enkidu (Tablet I): named, frank and unhurried, in plain pentameter: 'And so the harlot, Shamhat, showed him her breasts, / showed him her body. The hairy-bodied man / came over to her, and lay down on her, and then / she showed him the things a woman knows how to do.' (Poetry Foundation / PoemHunter excerpt of Tablet I). Ishtar's proposal (Tablet VI), built on Moran's crib: 'The goddess Ishtar saw him and fell in love / with the beauty of Gilgamesh and longed for his body', followed by a blunt 'Give me the seed of your body' (quoted in Bruce Gerig, 'David and Jonathan and the Epic of Gilgamesh'); Gilgamesh's catalogue of her discarded lovers is kept and played for wit. Enkidu's death and Gilgamesh's lament (Tablets VII to VIII): expanded and heavily weighted, with Gilgamesh grieving 'like a widow'. Siduri's advice (Tablet X): kept, following Speiser's use of the Old Babylonian text (eat, dance, wash, cherish the child and the wife), without any marker that it comes from a different recension. [uncertain: exact Ferry wording not verified] Utnapishtim's speech on mortality is rendered as plain aphorism: 'Time after time the river has risen and flooded. / The insect leaves the cocoon to live but a minute.' (quoted by Peseroff, Ploughshares). Death in the bedchamber (Tablet XI): after failing the sleep test Gilgamesh despairs that death lives in his bedroom and wherever he sets his foot; Ferry keeps the image in plain modern English. [uncertain: exact line not verified] Walls of Uruk: Gilgamesh returns with Urshanabi and shows him the walls, brickwork and fields, echoing the prologue, before the book moves on to Tablet XII.
diction_and_metre: Loose iambic pentameter in unrhymed two-line stanzas, flexible enough to take long, Speiser-derived speech lines and repetitions. Diction is modern, plain and spoken American English, with no archaism and no 'thee/thou'. Ferry keeps some of the formulaic repetition of the original (the repeated dreams, travel formulas, 'he spoke and said'), which some readers find laborious in the later tablets, but he also shortens and cuts. Punctuation is used expressively (semicolons in the opening act as a chant: 'who made the journey; heartbroken; reconciled;'). The tone mixes lyric elegy with dry irony; publisher copy calls it 'more lyrical than epic'.
sample_line: "The Story / of him who knew the most of all men know; / who made the journey; heartbroken; reconciled;" (Ferry, Gilgamesh, opening of Tablet I; Poetry Foundation excerpt)
critical_response: Finalist, National Book Critics Circle Award in Poetry (1992) per publisher materials; New York Times Notable Book. Tom Sleigh, New York Times Book Review: '[Ferry's] technical genius and literary sophistication evoke not only the hero's anguish, but the rage and despair of the untouchable.' D. S. Carne-Ross, The New Criterion: 'David Ferry has performed this service, and has given us a noble poem as close to the ancient original as we in our ignorance have any right to.' John Ray, Times Literary Supplement: 'Ferry's skill brings a fresh interpretation to the power of Gilgamesh.' Joyce Peseroff, Ploughshares no. 58 (Fall 1992), praised the blank-verse couplets for giving 'both freedom and structure'. Danny Yee's comparative review classes it with Mason as a 'freer version', 'not a translation but a transformation', presenting the epic 'much as if it were a work of English poetry', and says the choice between Mason and Ferry 'is likely to be a matter of taste'. It became a standard US classroom text (e.g. Boston University's Core Curriculum). [uncertain: NBCC finalist status appears in publisher/secondary copy; Wikipedia does not list it]
controversies: No serious dispute over provenance or authorship. The standing objection is category and accuracy: a poet without Akkadian producing a 'rendering' from Speiser and Moran's cribs, filling lacunae and silently merging recensions, so that readers cannot tell ancient text from Ferry's supplements. Assyriologically, it predates Andrew George's 2003 edition and so rests on a 1950s text. Some readers also object to its long repetitions and to omitted details. Ferry and the subtitle are candid ('A New Rendering', not 'translation'), which blunted criticism.
regional_reception: No evidence found of Arabic, Kurdish or Iraqi translation or reception. Its reach is English-language, largely American, mostly in universities and poetry circles. [uncertain]
ai_craft_tension: Ferry is the clearest case of the division of labour an AI essay could lean on. The philology was done by other people: Speiser's printed translation and Moran's word-for-word cribs were, in effect, a machine-readable intermediate. Ferry says outright that not knowing Babylonian helped, because the flat literal versions left room for him. What he added is exactly what a crib lacks: a verse form ('once I'd found a suitable form, iambic pentameter couplets'), a sense of which passages matter (Enkidu's death, Ishtar's proposition), and a compressed reading of the whole ('heartbroken; reconciled'). Today a model can produce a Speiser-grade crib from a transliteration in seconds, and can produce pentameter too. The question Ferry raises is whether a model would choose to put 'heartbroken; reconciled' in the first lines, or would know that the Enkidu lament is where the poem should be heaviest. The cost is also instructive: Ferry's clean couplets erase the gaps, the recension boundaries and the scholarship, so the reader gets a poem that feels whole when the tablets are not. That smoothing is precisely the risk people raise about fluent machine output.
essay_hooks: 1) The poet who could not read the tablets: 'I was working from scholarly word-for-word translations and these had the effect of being, in themselves, less nuanced and complex than I would have found the Babylonian, if I knew Babylonian' (Ferry, BU Core interview, 2010). 2) Speed: 'I did the whole thing in a matter of months. Time of my life.' (same interview). A version still in print after 30+ years, written in months, from a crib. 3) The human-in-the-loop pair: Moran (Harvard Assyriologist) hands over word-for-word versions of the opening and Ishtar's proposal; Ferry supplies the form. A 1990s precedent for 'machine translation plus poet'. 4) Two words that carry the arc: 'who made the journey; heartbroken; reconciled;' (opening lines). 5) Carne-Ross's backhanded praise: 'as close to the ancient original as we in our ignorance have any right to' (The New Criterion). 6) Danny Yee on Ferry and Mason: 'in the Mason and Ferry versions these specific lines can't really be identified', a neat line on how fluency hides the gaps. 7) Ferry's one-sentence character list for Gilgamesh: 'terrifying, big-hearted, arrogant, scared, joyful, humiliated, sexy, desperate, grieving, self-deceiving, learning, heartbroken, reconciled'.
